query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive model that explicitly incorporates defect states (including 1 wt.% oxygen contamination) and their effect on electron scattering in bulk HfNbTaTiZr will predict electrical conductivity in both the nearly 0–200 K regime (where quantum and defect scattering dominate) and the 300–1200 K regime (where phonon scattering is primary) with higher accuracy than conventional analytical methods that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy produced under conventional conditions with minimal processing-induced deviations, with a controlled variant containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.intervention: Application of an advanced predictive modeling framework that integrates defect-induced electron scattering and impurity effects (including oxygen-induced modifications of the electronic structure) into conductivity predictions.
generation.conditions: Electrical conductivity measured in two temperature ranges: low temperatures (0–200 K) where defect and quantum effects are significant, and high temperatures (300–1200 K) where phonon scattering dominates; experiments conducted on both nearly pure and 1 wt.% oxygen-contaminated samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Defect structures and oxygen impurity-related local electronic perturbations that increase electron scattering rates relative to predictions from a perfect crystal.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly modeling the impact of defects and oxygen impurities on the electronic density of states and scattering rates, the predictive approach reduces systematic errors seen in analytical models that assume ideal crystals; in low temperatures, enhanced defect scattering accounts for additional resistivity, while at high temperatures, the interplay of oxygen-induced carrier scattering and phonon interactions is captured.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will yield conductivity predictions that more closely match experimental measurements in both temperature regimes. Specifically, in the 0–200 K range, predicted conductivity will be lower than defect-free estimates (accounting for increased scattering), and in the 300–1200 K regime, the incorporation of oxygen effects will adjust the temperature dependence, leading to reduced prediction errors compared to conventional analytical predictions.
generation.baseline: Standard analytical models that assume perfect, defect-free crystal structures and ignore oxygen contamination, which tend to misestimate conductivity (often overestimating the values) particularly when significant defect scattering is present.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable to bulk samples of HfNbTaTiZr with homogeneously distributed defects and up to 1 wt.% oxygen. Its predictions are expected to be valid for temperature regimes from near 0 K up to 1200 K, but may require modification for nanostructured samples or oxygen levels significantly outside the 1 wt.% level.
generation.uncertainty: While the model is expected to account for defect and impurity scattering, the quantitative improvement in prediction accuracy remains uncertain without extensive calibration datasets. The precise magnitude of the improved accuracy (e.g., percent reduction in prediction error) is not yet determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples under controlled conditions, creating two sets – one near defect free and another intentionally alloyed to contain 1 wt.% oxygen. Measure the electrical conductivity of both sets across the temperature ranges 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Compare these experimental conductivity values with predictions from both the new predictive model and standard analytical models that assume defect-free conditions.
measurements: Electrical conductivity at selected temperatures (e.g., 50 K, 150 K, 300 K, 600 K, 900 K, 1200 K)
Microstructural and compositional analysis to confirm oxygen content and defect distribution
Statistical error metrics (e.g., RMSE, MAE) for model predictions versus experimental data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictive model does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in prediction error compared to the conventional analytical models (for example, failing to reduce RMSE by a pre-defined margin) across both temperature regimes, or if measured conductivity values fall outside the 95% confidence intervals of the model predictions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:2.4. Approaches to Alloy Design and Selection
cited_evidence.text: Each approach to alloy design (selection) that has been discussed above would give an alloy composition for which solidification path, volume fractions of phases and phase equilibria at different temperatures could be calculated, provided thermodynamic data was available. This task is not possible currently, for the reasons discussed in the introduction. Using knowledge gained from on-going research it is possible to make some informed predictions for the selected alloys. The latter and the calculated (predicted) properties can be tested experimentally. For example, the alloy A should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3 and Nbss should be stable at 1500 °C but not the C14 NbCr2 Laves and A15 intermetallic phases and the alloy should not pest. The alloy B should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, eutectic with Nbss and Nb5Si3 should form (see below), in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3, Nbss (most likely solid solution with no Si) and A15 intermetallic should be stable at 1500 °C but not C14 NbCr2 Laves phase and the alloy should not pest.

The structure of the paper is as follows. First the approach used to design and select the two alloys is explained. Then the experimental techniques used for the characterisation of the alloys are described. The results for the cast and heat treated alloys are presented before their isothermal oxidation at 800 and 1200 °C is presented. The discussion considers first the macrosegregation and microstructures of the alloys, which are also compared with High Entropy Alloys, and then their oxidation behaviour is considered.

Contamination by oxygen of phases below the scale and sometimes in the bulk of Nb-silicide-based alloys also has been reported in [,]. The presence of Ge containing compounds, with the exception of NbGe2, and A15 intermetallic below the scale (Table 5) is consistent with the data in [,,]. However, the absence of other Sn intermetallics (NbSn2, (Ti,Nb)6Sn5, and TM5Sn2Si), which were observed in [,], also should be noted. These observations would suggest (a) that the presence of Al and/or Cr is not essential for the formation of Ge and Sn containing intermetallic phases below the scale, and (b) that the alloying with RMs (synergy of Ta with W in this study) (i) suppresses the formation (stability ?) of certain Ge and Sn rich compounds below the scale, (ii) affects solute partitioning in Nb5Si3 below the scale (compare the data for Nb5(Si1-xGex)3 and W-rich Nb5(Si1-xGex)3 with that for Nb5Si3 and Ti-rich Nb5Si3 in Table 5) and promotes the formation (stability?) of NbGe2 below the scale. Further research is necessary to clarify (b).

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.1. Contamination of Nb with Interstitials
cited_evidence.text: Oxygen contents as high as 0.41 wt.% increased the room temperature tensile strength of Nb from 276 MPa to 896 PMa and reduced the elongation from 30 to 10%. Contamination of Nb with oxygen increased its hardness [] and caused embrittlement [,]. The latter has been attributed to screw dislocations moving through a repulsive field imposed by oxygen atoms, forming cross kinks and emitting excess vacancies in Nb which bind with oxygen and hinder dislocation motion []. Oxygen also affected the elevated temperature properties []. Tensile tests conducted on Nb with varying oxygen concentrations (10, 200 and 4300 wppm) revealed brittle failures below 400 °C for oxygen concentration of 0.43% []. At higher temperatures ductile failures were produced. The amount of ductility exhibited by Nb−O alloys at elevated temperatures was sensitive to strain-rate. For example, Nb containing 0.15% oxygen exhibited a decrease in the reduction in area from 90% to 30% at 467 °C due to a change in strain rate of 5 × 10−5 to 2 × 10−1 s−1 [].

In RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs, the CC bcc solid solutions with Ge+Sn and Al, Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti and W additions are (i) stable (Figure 1) and (ii) Si free [,]. It is suggested (a) that single phase bcc solid solution RCCAs or RHEAs with above elements would be stable at high temperatures. Furthermore, given that Ge+Sn with Al, Cr, Hf, Mo and Ti improve oxidation at pest and high temperatures [,,,] it is suggested (b) that these RCCAs or RHEAs would also be oxidation resistant. For B containing RM(Nb)ICs, RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs, RM(NB)ICs/RHEAs, RCCAs and RHEAs it is suggested to study the contamination with oxygen of their solid solutions and to find out if there is a relationship between the parameter δ and the oxygen concentration, see Boron Containing RM(Nb)ICs in Section 3.2.1.
